metadata.note: The New Orleans, Jackson and Great Northern (5 ft gauge, New Orleans - Ponchatoula - Brookhaven - Jackson - Canton, 206 mi, completed 1858) and its 1874-1877 successor over the same line, the New Orleans, St. Louis and Chicago. From 1877 the line is drawn by ic-cstlno-general in illinois_central.geojson. The NOJ&GN is drawn in three sections because each has different proven war years. Research report: research/branches/new_orleans_jackson_and_great_northern_railroad.txt.

Colours are new, picked by script for maximum distance from all ~930 colours in use and distinct from IC orange #F4801F. Known defect NOT fixed here (out of scope): illinois_central.geojson ic-cstlno-general, Panama Limited and City of New Orleans, and amtrak.geojson City of New Orleans 1971-1995, draw Jackson - Memphis on the post-10 Sep 1995 Amtrak route via Yazoo City/Greenwood instead of the IC Grenada District via Canton - Durant - Grenada; Canton is ~17 mi off those lines. not_yet_sourced: [OPEN] start, New Orleans - Ponchatoula 1855: the depot year; Hennick's 1854 mixed-train / 'regular passenger service' citations (DP Oct-Nov 1854) have a garbled destination. First passenger year and how far north trains ran in 1854-57 not established (Daily Picayune 1854-58 or the NOJ&GN annual reports of 1856-59 would settle it).
[OPEN] start, Ponchatoula - Brookhaven 1858: completion year of the through line; staged openings to Osyka (c.1855-56?) and on to Brookhaven (1857?) not established.
[OPEN] end, Brookhaven - Canton 1863: last confirmed year; 1864 is a withheld unknown. 1865 rests on a single [ANCHOR] (June 1865 passenger-car use).
Jackson - Canton completion: 1856 (one search summary, Wikipedia-mirror wording) vs 1858 (Ridgeland marker; overall completion sources). 1858 adopted.

Jan 1866 tri-weekly mixed train (Hennick): endpoints not named; assumed New Orleans - Canton. If Ponchatoula - Brookhaven was not yet rebuilt, that section's restart could be late 1866 or 1867. The full 1866 annual report would settle it.
1877 foreclosure sale date: 16 May 1877 (ICC valuation) vs 17 Mar 1877 (SNAC, via search). Irrelevant to whole-year drawing.
Whether the June 1862 'MAIL' train carried civilian passengers - the sheet never says 'passenger'.
Estaville, 'A Strategic Railroad', Louisiana History 14:2 (1973) - the standard history of the road's war - not read; may confirm or overturn the 1862-65 treatment.
In-city New Orleans alignment of the 1855-1892 approach to Calliope & Clara not researched (drawn on the later UPT approach).
All headways and speeds are estimates.
source_conflicts: Charter dates: Louisiana Act 148 of 22 Apr 1853 (Hennick) vs 'chartered on April 22, 1852' (msrailroads); Mississippi 25 Feb 1852 (Hennick) vs 11 Mar 1852 (ICC valuation).
New Orleans terminal: 'substantial passenger depot' at Calliope & Clara, DP 5 Dec 1855 (Hennick) vs Fowler 'New Orleans (1st) 1858>1892' (likely Fowler's 1858-Dinsmore floor).
1877 sale: 16 May (ICC) vs 17 Mar (SNAC; existing IC note 'Mar 1877').
Hennick dates 'regular passenger service to Jackson' to DP 21 Nov 1854 - impossible (the line reached Jackson in 1858); his page also heads the road 4 ft 8 1/2 in though it was 5 ft until 1881.
metadata.freight_only_audit: Nothing freight-only drawn: wartime years with only military/freight use trimmed (New Orleans - Ponchatoula 1862-65, Ponchatoula - Brookhaven 1863-65 after spring 1863); the unbuilt Canton - Aberdeen extension not drawn.
metadata.line_label_audit: Labels written to Rule 6 at creation.

properties.line: New Orleans, Jackson and Great Northern: New Orleans – Ponchatoula
properties.speed_source: Estimate, unsourced for peacetime. The only timing read is the Confederate 'Time Table No. 1' of 22 Jun 1862: Mail North dep. Ponchatoula 7.00am, arr. Canton 6.20pm, 159 mi in 11 h 20 min = about 23 km/h (wartime). 25 km/h is an estimate for a 5 ft gauge 1850s-70s road.
properties.geometry_source: OpenStreetMap via Overpass (maps.mail.ru mirror, 2026-11-12), routed with opstrace.py: old_railway_operator=IC ways (CN McComb Subdivision New Orleans - Jackson; 'Grenada Railway' Jackson - Canton, the old IC Grenada District) plus untagged CN McComb Subdivision ways and the UPT approach. Waypoints are Nominatim town geocodes, with Tangipahoa (returned the parish), Madison (returned the county) and Bogue Chitto (returned the Neshoba County place) hand-pinned to their OSM place nodes, and the New Orleans end pinned to Calliope & Clara.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced 48.2 mi against 47 mi documented (New Orleans - Ponchatoula 47 mi; 1866 NOJ&GN annual report section mileages). Routed by opstrace.py over OSM: whole New Orleans - Canton trace 206.8 mi before simplification: 202.2 mi on old_railway_operator=IC ways (CN McComb Subdivision; 'Grenada Railway', the ex-IC Grenada District, Jackson - Canton), 2.9 mi on untagged rail (CN McComb Subdivision pieces without the historic tag; UPT approach), 1.8 mi on ways tagged old_railway_operator=KCS - the shared New Orleans Union Passenger Terminal approach tracks, not a KCS route; north of Magnolia about 2.5 mi runs on OSM railway=abandoned 'McComb Subdivision' ways, the lifted second main track beside the live line. Straight-line legs: none. Waypoint fit: Calliope & Clara end 0.3 km from the pinned point (in the UPT throat); Kenner 2.0 km (town centroid), Frenier 0.1, Manchac 0.0, Ponchatoula 0.0 km. Ponchatoula falls at traced mile 48.2 from Calliope & Clara (documented 47). LATER ALIGNMENT, New Orleans: the 1855-1892 passenger terminal was the depot at Calliope & Clara Sts (Hennick, DP 5 Dec 1855; Fowler 'New Orleans (1st) 1858>1892'). The trace ends at a reconstructed Calliope & Clara point (-90.0845, 29.9485: the two streets no longer meet; the intersection is extrapolated from the surviving pieces of both, +/- ~200 m), which sits on the Union Passenger Terminal approach about 0.3 mi west of the UPT platforms, so the terminal end is honest. But the in-city approach from about Kenner to that point is the 20th-century IC / 1954 UPT approach (OSM 'New Orleans Union Passenger Terminal' / Back Belt corridor); the 1850s line's own route through Carrollton and the uptown streets was not researched and may differ by several blocks to a mile. LATER STRUCTURE, Manchac: the swamp crossing and Pass Manchac bridge are drawn on the modern CN McComb Subdivision embankment - the same corridor, but in 1860 this stretch was still trestle/low fill 'being filled and raised' (1866 annual report), not today's structure. Relocations: none detected - a scan of IC-tagged abandoned ways within 3 km of the line found only the lifted second track north of Magnolia (same corridor), short spurs at Jackson and a branch stub at Brookhaven; no bypassed main-line alignment at Hammond, McComb or Jackson shows in OSM. LATER-ALIGNMENT NOTE: the drawn track is the CN line as it is today; any curve easing, grade separation or double-tracking since the 1850s-70s was not checked. 5 ft gauge until 29 Jul 1881; the drawn track is the standard-gauge successor on the same corridor.

segments.note: [OPEN start] NOJ&GN's own trains, New Orleans (Calliope & Clara depot) - Kenner - Manchac - Ponchatoula, the first section built (Pass Manchac bridge opened May 1854). 1855 is NOT a known opening: it is the year of the 'substantial passenger depot' at Calliope & Clara (Hennick citing the Daily Picayune, 5 Dec 1855). Hennick's DP citations also put two coaches (Oct 1854), 'a mixed train daily' (22 Oct 1854) and 'regular passenger service' (21 Nov 1854) on the road in 1854, but his destination text is garbled ('to Jackson', impossible in 1854), so 1854 is withheld. The 1857 earnings ('freight, passengers, and mails') independently prove passengers by 1857. Ends April 1862: on 24 Apr 1862, as Farragut passed the forts, Confederate Gen. Lovell took the rolling stock north of Ponchatoula, and for the rest of the war Ponchatoula was the road's southern terminal (1866 annual report; csa-railroads). 1862-1865 is NOT drawn: Federal military use of this section is shown only for 1865 and no civilian passenger service is evidenced (report blocks [5], [7]). Do not extend without evidence. Headway estimated: one passenger (or mixed) train each way daily, after the June 1862 timetable's single MAIL pair and Hennick's 'daily service began March 12 [1866]'; no prewar or 1866-74 timetable has been read for frequency.
sources: Segment-level: research/branches/new_orleans_jackson_and_great_northern_railroad.txt blocks [1], [5], [7] - Hennick App. III p.f1 citing Daily Picayune 18 May 1854, 10 Oct 1854, 22 Oct 1854, 21 Nov 1854, 5 Dec 1855 (start); NOJ&GN Eleventh Annual Report, 1 Mar 1866 (1857 earnings; Lovell's 24 Apr 1862 removal of rolling stock); csa-railroads.com (Ponchatoula southern terminal for the rest of the war). Headway estimated.

segments.note: NOJ&GN's own trains after the war. The company took the road back on 24 Jun 1865 (1866 annual report); Hennick: 'a tri-weekly mixed train began running Jan. 20, 1866. Daily service began March 12 the same year' - endpoints not named, assumed through New Orleans - Canton (one secondary source; see metadata.not_yet_sourced). June 1869 Official Guide table reproduced on msrailroads.com (existence only; image not read). P. G. T. Beauregard president 1866-1870; H. S. McComb control from April 1870 was a change of ownership, not of operator - the NOJ&GN still ran its own trains, so no split. From 1871 Chicago through trains hauled Pullman cars to New Orleans via the Mississippi Central and IC (Hennick). Ends 13 Apr 1874 with consolidation into the New Orleans, St. Louis and Chicago (ICC valuation), which continued the service (feature noslc-new-orleans-canton). Headway estimated: one passenger (or mixed) train each way daily, after the June 1862 timetable's single MAIL pair and Hennick's 'daily service began March 12 [1866]'; no prewar or 1866-74 timetable has been read for frequency.

segments.note: [OPEN start] NOJ&GN's own trains, Ponchatoula - Tickfaw - Amite - Tangipahoa - Osyka - Magnolia - Summit - Bogue Chitto - Brookhaven. 1858 is the year the through line was completed - the earliest year this section is PROVEN in passenger use - NOT its opening: Osyka is said by local histories to have been the northern terminus for about two years before 1858 (c.1855-57), unsourced from any primary. Wartime: under Confederate military control from April 1862 (same company running the trains, so no split). The Confederate 'Time Table No. 1' of 22 Jun 1862 runs one daily MAIL each way Ponchatoula - Canton through every station on this section (the sheet calls it 'Mail', not 'passenger'; in 1862 practice that was the passenger train). Ends spring 1863: 'From that point [Ponchatoula] to Brookhaven ... the road had not been used since the spring of 1863' (1866 annual report). 1864-1865 not drawn: unused, bridges burnt (report block [7]). Headway estimated: one passenger (or mixed) train each way daily, after the June 1862 timetable's single MAIL pair and Hennick's 'daily service began March 12 [1866]'; no prewar or 1866-74 timetable has been read for frequency.

McComb City founded 1872 as the NOJ&GN shops town (chartered 5 Apr 1872 by H. S. McComb). Ends 13 Apr 1874, consolidation into the New Orleans, St. Louis and Chicago (ICC valuation). segments.note: [OPEN end] NOJ&GN's own trains, Brookhaven - Hazlehurst - Crystal Springs - Terry - Byram - Jackson - Tougaloo - Madison - Calhoun (Gluckstadt) - Canton, junction with the Mississippi Central. Through line completed 1858 (Ridgeland marker: 'first railroad built in Madison County, completed in 1858'; Tougaloo carries Fowler's x = 1858 Dinsmore letter). A conflicting search summary says Canton - Jackson was 'completed in 1856' - recorded, not adopted. Canton was the company's wartime domicile from 27 Aug 1862; under Confederate military control 1862-65 (same company ran the trains - no split). Time Table No. 1 (22 Jun 1862) times the daily MAIL Brookhaven - Jackson - Canton. Jackson captured 14 May 1863 and track torn up north and south of it; 2.5 mi south of Jackson torn up 'since May, 1863'. 1863 is the last CONFIRMED year, NOT a known end: no source dates when passenger trains stopped, and 1864 is a withheld unknown, not a known suspension. Do not extend without evidence. segments.note: 1865 is an [ANCHOR]: in June 1865 the road Jackson - Canton, 'though much out of repair ... was still being used', with '1 first-class and 2 second-class passenger cars' fit for use, and Brookhaven - Jackson 'though dilapidated, was in use' with '4 box cars, one of which was used for passengers' (1866 annual report, describing the road as received back on 24 Jun 1865). Passengers were certainly carried in 1865, but the 2.5-mi Jackson gap was not closed until mid/late 1865 ('in the short space of thirteen days'), so Brookhaven - Jackson and Jackson - Canton were separate operations for part of the year. From 1866 continuous NOJ&GN service as on the rest of the line (Hennick: tri-weekly mixed 20 Jan 1866, daily 12 Mar 1866; June 1869 Official Guide). Ends 13 Apr 1874, consolidation into the New Orleans, St. Louis and Chicago (ICC valuation). segments.note: The New Orleans, St. Louis and Chicago was formed by articles of consolidation of 13 Apr 1874 between the NOJ&GN and the Mississippi Central (ICC valuation), the first single company over New Orleans - Canton - Jackson, Tenn. Fowler's y = 1875 Official Guide letter is on nearly every station New Orleans - Canton (Kenner, Manchac, Ponchatoula, Hammond, Amite, Tangipahoa, Osyka, Magnolia, McComb City, Summit, Bogue Chitto, Brookhaven, Hazlehurst, Crystal Springs, Terry, Byram, Jackson, Tougaloo, Madison, Calhoun, Canton). A receiver was appointed 11 Mar 1876 and operated the property through 1876 - the same trains under the same name, so NOT a split. The NOJ&GN portion was sold under foreclosure in 1877 - 16 May 1877 (ICC valuation) or 17 Mar 1877 (SNAC record via search; the existing IC note says 'Mar 1877') - and reorganised as the New Orleans, Jackson and Northern, IC-controlled; that sub-year interlude has no feature of its own. It was consolidated in Nov 1877 into the Chicago, St. Louis and New Orleans, drawn from 1877 by ic-cstlno-general in illinois_central.geojson. Headway estimated: one passenger (or mixed) train each way daily, after the June 1862 timetable's single MAIL pair and Hennick's 'daily service began March 12 [1866]'; no prewar or 1866-74 timetable has been read for frequency. Through cars to Chicago over the Mississippi Central/IC very probably meant more than one train a day; not established.
